newsitem.title: USA: US Crude Outlook - Bears return on Iraq news, OPEC.
newsitem.headline: US Crude Outlook - Bears return on Iraq news, OPEC.

text.p: U.S. crude prices could head to lower levels this week on news the UN-Iraq "oil-for-food" deal may be on the verge of getting done, and views OPEC will retain its current production ceiling, industry sources said.
Still, forecasts for below-normal temperatures coupled with lean hydrocarbon inventories across the board, promise to keep the market volatile, they said.
"Many feel that with the election out of the way, the oil deal is ready to get done," said Gerald Samuels, an oil trader and managing director of ARB Oil.
Samuels was echoing views held by other players that the U.S. presidential election, among other factors, had been clouding implementation of the Iraqi limited oil sales.

Statements from Nizar Hamdoon, Iraqi ambassador to the U.N., that Baghdad agreed to all conditions necessary to implement limited Iraqi oil sales appeared to be adding downward pressure to prices on Monday.

Still, spot West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude in Cushing, Oklahoma was trading late Monday 25 cents lower in the $23.45-23.55 a barrel range on statements earlier in the day by Hamdoon and U.S. officials oil sales were ever closer.
"I think the tendency if anything is to drift lower," said Rita Beale, an analyst at Houston-based Fimat Futures USA Inc. "But the market is choppy, without a lot of direction."
Beale said outright prices are trading in a range, with a resistance level of $24.55 a barrel for January West Texas Intermediate (WTI). "I can't get bullish until prices break past that," she said.

Adding to the bearishness were virtually unanimous views the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) is likely to roll over its existing 25.03 million per day (bpd) output quota at its ministerial meeting this week in Vienna.

Analysts note the bearishness of this scenario lies in the fact that quota busting by some members, notably Venezuela and Nigeria, threatens to douse what would otherwise be considered robust petroleum demand worldwide.
"The spreads have weakened, we could see more selling than we are seeing now," a trader said, noting further news on Iraq oil sales or an OPEC rollover could add downward pressure.

On the weather front, Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis forecasted temperatures to be six to 12 degress below normal from the U.S. Rocky Mountain region to the East Coast through the end of the month.
While corresponding demand for heating oil amid low inventories could fuel price gains this week, broader bearish factors are likely to seize the day, players said.
Ken Miller, senior principal at Houston-based Purvin & Gertz, echoed Beale's bearish sentiment.
Despite low inventories, this week's stocks report from the American Petroleum Institute (API) might not be as bullish as some market players believe, Miller said.
"There's a lot of consumer stocking going on. Even though you've got a possible cold snap, you won't see such a big draw on Tuesday."
"I'm a contrarian this week," one trader said. "I think heating oil is going to keep the market firm."
